title.en: Enforce joint limits in the model, not in the pose

summary: Clamp articulation to the axes and ranges the joint actually permits before the pose reaches the renderer.
objective: Keep articulated anatomy and mechanisms from producing poses their joints cannot reach.
applies_when: A skeleton, limb or mechanism is posed interactively or by a solver.
A joint is described by name, such as hinge, pivot or ball and socket.
Motion is driven by data, physics or inverse kinematics rather than by hand.
example_prompts: Let me pose the knee but stop it bending the wrong way.
Constrain the arm joints to realistic motion.
negative_signals: Stylised characters whose exaggerated articulation is deliberate.
Purely decorative rigs with no anatomical or mechanical claim.
not_for: Stylised characters whose exaggerated articulation is deliberate.
Purely decorative rigs with no anatomical or mechanical claim.

principles: A joint has an axis structure, not just a range. A hinge joint permits bending and straightening about a single axis, while a ball and socket joint is multiaxial, so allowing three free rotations at a hinge is already wrong before any limit is considered.

Flexion decreases the angle at a joint and extension increases it; extension beyond the normal range is hyperextension, which in a body is described as abnormal or injurious rather than as a valid pose.
Limits belong to the model because several consumers depend on them: the interactive handle, the inverse-kinematic solver, the animation retarget and any physical constraint.
Clamping in the renderer hides the violation instead of preventing it, and leaves the underlying state outside the valid set.
implementation: Give each joint an explicit type, axis or axes, and a range for each degree of freedom, stored with the model rather than in the pose data.
Apply the constraint when the state is set, so the stored joint values are always inside the permitted set.
Make a solver respect the limits during iteration rather than clamping only its final answer, otherwise the reported residual is misleading.
Show the constraint to the user, for example by resisting a drag at the limit and displaying the current angle.
Mark deliberately exaggerated joints as stylistic so a limit violation is not mistaken for a bug.
observable_checks: Drag each joint past its limit and confirm the stored value, not just the drawn pose, stops at the boundary.
Check a hinge for unintended rotation about the other two axes.
Run the solver towards an unreachable target and confirm it reports the residual rather than passing through the limit.
Play back imported motion data and confirm out-of-range frames are reported instead of silently absorbed.

creative_affordances: Invented anatomy can have any joint structure; declare it and constrain it consistently.
A comparison mode that shows an unconstrained pose next to a constrained one is a strong teaching device.
known_limits: Authored articulation guidance citing joint-type and movement definitions; it asserts no numerical range of motion for any specific joint.
Real ranges vary with individual, age, load and coupling between joints, which this rule does not model.

claims.statement: Hinge and pivot joints are uniaxial, permitting motion in a single plane such as flexion and extension or rotation, while ball and socket joints are multiaxial; flexion decreases the angle at a joint, extension increases it, and hyperextension is extension beyond the normal range of motion and is described as abnormal or injurious.
claims.scope: Human joint classification and movement terminology; no numerical range of motion is given.
